title: Commonsense_knowledge_(artificial_intelligence)
summary:
In artificial intelligence research, commonsense knowledge consists of facts about the everyday world, such as "Lemons are sour" or "Cows say moo," that all humans are expected to know. It is currently an unsolved problem in artificial general intelligence. The first AI program to address common sense knowledge was Advice Taker in 1959 by John McCarthy.

Commonsense knowledge can underpin a commonsense reasoning process, to attempt inferences such as "You might bake a cake because you want people to eat the cake." Common sense knowledge also helps to solve problems in the face of incomplete information. Using widely held beliefs about everyday objects, AI systems make common sense assumptions or default assumptions about the unknown similar to the way people do. For example, if we know "Tweety is a bird," because we know "typically birds fly," we may reasonably assume "Tweety can fly." As more knowledge is discovered, the AI system can revise its assumptions. If we later learn "Tweety is a penguin," truth maintenance revises this assumption because "penguins do not fly."

Compared with humans, all existing computer programs that attempt human-level AI perform extremely poorly on modern commonsense reasoning benchmark tests such as the Winograd Schema Challenge. The problem of attaining human-level competency at commonsense knowledge tasks is considered to probably be AI-complete, meaning solving it would require the ability to synthesize a fully human-level intelligence.

Compiling comprehensive knowledge bases of commonsense assertions (CSKBs) is a long-standing challenge in AI research. From early expert-driven efforts like CYC and WordNet, significant advances were achieved via the crowdsourced OpenMind Commonsense project, which led to the crowdsourced ConceptNet knowledge base. Several approaches have attempted to automate CSKB construction, most notably via text mining (WebChild, Quasimodo, TransOMCS, Ascent), as well as harvesting these directly from pre-trained language models (AutoTOMIC). Applications include MIT's BullySpace extension of ConceptNet to catch taunting social media comments, chatbots, computers that compose original fiction, and intelligent software agents at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory used to detect violations of a comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty.
